PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: a minimum wage a fifth higher.

Your turn. New Jersey's minimum wage rises nineteen percent; Pennsylvania's stays put. By November, how did employment in New Jersey's restaurants compare with Pennsylvania's? It fell by a tenth; it fell by a few percent, as modest textbook elasticities suggest; it did not change; or it rose. Pause, and choose.

The answer is D. In February, New Jersey's restaurants employed 20.44 full-time equivalents each, Pennsylvania's 23.33. By November, New Jersey's had 21.03 and Pennsylvania's had fallen to 21.17. Pennsylvania is the counterfactual: what would have happened to New Jersey without the rise. Comparing the changes, the difference in differences, New Jersey gained 2.75 employees per restaurant relative, with a standard error of 1.34. About 11 percent more jobs, as the starting wage rose about 11 percent. These are Card and Krueger's numbers, recomputed here from their published data, to the second decimal.
Supply: Start with a worker on the Island choosing how many hours to work. More hours mean more to spend and less time for everything else. The choice, written out: enjoy consumption, dislike hours, and earn the wage on every hour worked, plus some income from elsewhere. A higher wage pulls two ways. Each hour now buys more, so work more: the substitution effect. But you are richer, and can afford more time off: the income effect. For this worker the substitution effect wins at low wages and the income effect above about 14 dollars an hour, so the supply curve bends backwards: one reason hours in rich countries fell as wages rose over the twentieth century.

So 'how much do people respond to pay' has three answers, and economists mix them up at their peril. The Marshallian elasticity: raise the wage and nothing else. For this worker it is +0.16 at six dollars and -0.11 at thirty. Strip out the income effect and what remains is the Hicksian, or compensated, elasticity: +0.39 and +0.30, positive at both. It is the one that measures the harm of a tax, because taxes are spent on something. And the Frisch elasticity, 0.5, answers a temporary rise: work hard while pay is high, rest when it is low. It is the number business-cycle models need.

Hours are one margin; whether to work at all is the other. If people differ in the lowest wage at which work is worth it, the share who work rises with the wage, along this curve. Raj Chetty, Adam Guren, Day Manoli and Andrea Weber pulled together the quasi-experimental evidence in 2011: permanent, Hicksian elasticities of about 0.3 for hours and 0.25 for participation, and Frisch elasticities of about 0.5 and 0.25. Modest numbers, and an order of magnitude below what business-cycle models need to explain the swings in hours by workers' choices alone.
Cabs: Chapter three. Do people choose their hours?

Most people cannot choose their hours from day to day. Cab drivers can, and their days differ: rain, conventions and holidays make some days pay far more than others. If drivers aim for a fixed amount each day, say three hundred dollars, and stop when they reach it, a busy day is a short day: hours fall as hourly earnings rise, with an elasticity of minus one. The standard model says the opposite: when an hour pays more, work more of them, and rest on slow days.

What do drivers do? In 1997 Colin Camerer, Linda Babcock, George Loewenstein and Richard Thaler studied New York drivers' trip sheets and found hours falling on high-earning days, as if drivers had daily targets, a famous result for behavioural economics. In 2015 Henry Farber used every New York taxi trip over five years and found drivers working more when the pay was better, with the drivers who stayed in the business responding most. And in 2021 Joshua Angrist, Sydnee Caldwell and Jonathan Hall ran an experiment, offering Boston's Uber drivers random cuts in the platform's fee: a Frisch elasticity of about 1.2, more than twice the survey estimates. Where hours are flexible, people respond to pay much as the standard model says.
Demand: Chapter four. Labour demand and a wage floor.

Now the employers. A firm hires another worker as long as that worker adds more to revenue than to cost, so the demand for labour is the value of the marginal worker, falling as more are hired. In a competitive market, with many firms and many workers, the wage settles where demand meets supply: here 8.55 dollars an hour. In 1946 George Stigler spelled out what a minimum wage above that does. Firms move up their demand curves and hire fewer: with a floor nineteen percent higher and a demand elasticity of a half, employment falls about 8 percent. More people want work at the higher wage, so unemployment opens up in between. That is the textbook prediction New Jersey was supposed to confirm, and its size depends on one number, the elasticity of demand.
Border: First, did the law bite? Here are the starting wages restaurants reported. In February, in both states, many paid exactly the old minimum, four twenty-five, and most paid less than five oh five: 91 percent in New Jersey. By November New Jersey's distribution had jumped: almost nobody paid below the new minimum, and 89 percent paid exactly five dollars and five cents. Pennsylvania's barely moved. The law bound hard, on almost every New Jersey restaurant, and yet employment did not fall.

Where did the cost go? Partly into prices: the price of an entrée rose about 3 percent in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania. The result provoked a fierce reply. David Neumark and William Wascher argued that telephone answers about employment were noisy, collected payroll records from 230 restaurants, and found employment about 4.6 percent lower in New Jersey. Card and Krueger answered with the government's own payroll-tax records, which showed no relative loss, and traced the difference to a handful of restaurants owned by a single franchisee. Twenty-five years of designs followed: neighbouring counties across state lines, panels of states, synthetic controls. The next chapter shows the one that changed the conversation.
Bunching: Chapter six. Missing jobs, excess jobs.

In 2019 Doruk Cengiz, Arindrajit Dube, Attila Lindner and Ben Zipperer counted jobs differently. Here is an illustrative distribution of jobs by their hourly wage. Raise the minimum to ten dollars. Jobs that paid less must either disappear or be paid more. So count the jobs that vanish below the new minimum, and the jobs that appear at and just above it. The employment effect is the difference. Jobs that paid well above the minimum should not move, so they check the comparison.

Across 138 state increases from 1979 to 2016, the jobs missing below each new minimum were matched by jobs appearing just above it: the number of low-wage jobs was essentially unchanged five years later. Their elasticity of employment with respect to low-wage pay is 0.41, with a standard error of 0.43: zero cannot be ruled out, but large losses can. Seattle is the warning. When it raised its minimum to 11 dollars and then 13, high relative to local pay, a team at the University of Washington found hours at low wages falling, mostly for the least experienced, with elasticities between -2.0 and -0.2, mostly in hours rather than jobs. The evidence fits a pattern: moderate minimums cost few jobs; high ones, relative to local wages, can.
Monopsony: In 1933 Joan Robinson gave a name to the opposite case: monopsony, a market with one buyer. If one firm employs most of a town, it faces the town's whole supply curve. To hire one more worker it must raise the wage, and pay the higher wage to everyone it already employs, so the cost of one more worker rises faster than the wage. The firm hires where that cost equals what the worker adds. So it hires fewer people, at a lower wage, than a competitive market would: 136 workers at 5.15 dollars instead of 215 at 5.99. With a supply elasticity of 3, wages are marked down 25 percent below what the marginal worker adds. Alan Manning argued in 2003 that firms need not be alone in town to have this power: if finding another job takes time, every employer faces an upward-sloping supply.

Now impose a minimum wage on the monopsonist. Below its own wage, nothing happens. Between its wage and the competitive one, the minimum removes the reason to hold back: the firm no longer raises everyone's pay by hiring one more, so it hires everyone willing to work at the minimum, and employment rises. Only above the competitive wage does the textbook's loss appear. So the effect of a minimum wage depends on how much power employers have, which is measured by how elastic the supply of workers to a single firm is. Anna Sokolova and Todd Sorensen collected about eight hundred estimates and found the answer varies by method, country and occupation; it is the next chapter's question.
IslandBorder: Chapter eight. The same design on the Island.

Which world was New Jersey in? On the Island the truth is known, so run the same design there, with 331 and 79 restaurants and the same rise, two hundred times in each world. When restaurants hire on competitive demand curves, the design finds job losses: -0.045 on average, negative in 83 percent of runs. When restaurants set their own wages, the same design finds gains, +0.197 on average, and never a loss. The method can tell the worlds apart. New Jersey's +0.102 sits with the monopsony runs. But one run's standard error is about four and a half points, so a single study can land in the wrong place: the reason one border study, however careful, did not settle the question, and why the evidence had to accumulate.
Mincer: Chapter nine. Human capital and Mincer's equation.

Wages differ for reasons beyond supply and demand in one market: people differ in what they can do. In 1964 Gary Becker called the skills people invest in human capital: like a machine, schooling costs something now, in fees and forgone earnings, and pays later. Here are 3,010 young American men in 1976, from a survey David Card later used: their average log wage by years of school. The points lie roughly on a straight line, about 5 percent more per year of school, before anything else is taken into account. There are bumps at twelve and sixteen years, a high-school and a college degree: diplomas themselves seem to pay.

In 1974 Jacob Mincer turned the investment idea into one of the most estimated equations in economics. The log wage is linear in years of school, and rises with years of experience at a diminishing rate. Fitted to 526 workers in the 1976 Current Population Survey, a year of school is worth 9.0 percent, with a standard error under one point. Experience adds about 4 percent a year at first, flattening as skills stop growing, to a peak after about 29 years. The equation explains only 30 percent of the differences in wages: people with the same schooling and experience earn very different amounts.

That makes the shape one of the series' facts. In the data, log wages rise close to a straight line with schooling. The theory: schooling is an investment repaid in wages. But a regression cannot tell us whether school makes people more productive, or whether the more able stay in school longer. The next chapter tries to find out.
Returns: Chapter ten. The return to schooling.

The worry has a name: ability bias. If abler people both stay longer in school and earn more, the regression credits school with what ability did. Among 935 men in a 1980 survey, least squares gives 0.075 a year. Add their IQ scores and it falls to 0.056: each extra year of school goes with an IQ about 3.5 points higher. The formula says the bias is positive. But a test score is a poor measure of ability, and school itself raises test scores, so controls cannot settle it. The field turned to natural experiments.

In 1995 David Card used geography. Young men who grew up near a four-year college were more likely to go, getting almost a year more school, and earned more. If living near a college matters for wages only through schooling, it is an instrument. With Card's controls, least squares gives 0.075; the instrument gives 0.131, with a standard error of 0.054. Recomputed here from his data, the published numbers come back. The instrumental estimate is larger, not smaller, than least squares, the opposite of what ability bias predicts.

Other designs agree. Joshua Angrist and Alan Krueger noticed in 1991 that children born early in the year reach the school-leaving age with less schooling, and that compulsory schooling kept up to 25 percent of would-be dropouts in school; their instrumental estimates were close to least squares. John Bound, David Jaeger and Regina Baker then showed that quarter of birth moves schooling so little that random numbers, used as instruments, gave similar answers: the lesson of weak instruments, now taught in every course. Philip Oreopoulos used Britain's rise in the school-leaving age from 14 to 15 in 1947, which kept almost half of fourteen-year-olds in school a year longer, and found large returns. Across designs, a year of school is worth roughly six to fifteen percent, and the natural experiments sit at or above least squares.
Roy: Every wage we observe was chosen. In 1951 Andrew Roy imagined an economy of fishers and hunters, each person good at each to a different degree, each choosing the trade that paid them more. On the Island, each dot is a person and their two possible wages, as a fisher or at the boatyard. Each picks the larger, after the cost of switching. The fishers we see earn more as fishers than the average islander would: 2.69 against 2.60 in logs. The boatbuilders, even more so: 2.88 against 2.50. Comparing the two trades' observed wages says little about what anyone would earn after a switch.

In 1979 James Heckman showed how to undo the selection. First, model who chooses which trade; then add to the wage regression a term, the inverse Mills ratio, that measures how selected each person is. On the Island, the truth, the average fishing wage across everyone, is 2.599. The fishers we see average 2.692. Heckman's two steps give 2.594. The correction works because something, here the cost of switching, moves people between trades without changing what they could earn in either. Without such a variable the method leans on the normal distribution. Part thirty-nine meets selection again in the gender gap, where who works shapes the wages we see.
Mariel: Chapter twelve. Immigration: the Mariel boatlift.

Immigration poses Card and Krueger's question from the other side: what happens to wages when the number of workers jumps? In April 1980 Fidel Castro allowed Cubans who wished to leave to depart from the port of Mariel. From May to September about 125,000 reached Miami by boat. Miami's labour force grew 7 percent almost overnight, its Cuban labour force 20 percent. Most of the newcomers had little schooling, so the supply of less-skilled workers rose even more. If any shock should lower wages, this one should.

What happened? In 1990 David Card compared Miami with four cities whose economies had moved with it before 1980, and found no measurable effect on less-skilled workers' wages or unemployment. In 2017 George Borjas looked at a narrower group, non-Hispanic men without a high-school diploma, and found their wages fell 10 to 30 percent. Giovanni Peri and Vasil Yasenov built a synthetic Miami from many cities and found no significant difference, adding that very small subsamples of a survey can produce large differences in either direction. The debate turned on who counts as a competing worker and how many of them a survey actually interviewed. Many studies now compare groups with the same schooling and experience across the whole country instead; their answers turn on how easily newcomers and natives substitute for each other, the elasticity Part thirty-nine measures for skilled and unskilled workers.
Frontier: Chapter fifteen. Frontier: concentration, non-competes, high minimums.

The frontier begins with the level. America's federal minimum has been 7.25 dollars an hour since 2009; in today's prices it peaked at 14.65 in 1968. States and cities now set their own, and some are far above anything studied in the 1990s: in 2024 California set twenty dollars for large fast-food chains. The evidence of this part was gathered mostly at moderate levels, and Seattle suggests the effects grow with the level. Where the line lies is the question for the next decade.

The open questions. Employer concentration: where a few firms do most of a town's hiring, are wages lower, and should antitrust care about labour markets as well as product markets? Non-compete agreements, which stop workers from joining a rival: in 2024 America's Federal Trade Commission adopted a rule banning most of them, but a federal court set it aside, and it never took effect. High minimums: where do the losses begin? The return to college: is it falling for the marginal student? And platform work, where hours are free and the platform sets the pay.
